## IVF: skip the regions you don't care about

HNSW is great but it has two real costs. ... For very large corpora or for systems that need to re-index often, the other classic approach is IVF, for Inverted File Index, adapted from text search.

The idea: cluster all the vectors into $k$ k groups with $k$ k-means (typically $k \approx \sqrt{N}$ k≈ N​). Each cluster has a centroid. When you index a new vector, assign it to the closest centroid and push it into that centroid's list. When you query, compute the distance from $q$ q to every centroid (cheap: only $k$ k of them), then only search inside the $p$ p closest centroid lists. That $p$ p is called `nprobe`.

Search a few inverted lists

Swipe or scroll to explore the diagram.

Intuition: only search the cells near the query, skip the rest of the map. IVF with six clusters — squares are centroids, dots are indexed vectors, the green dots are the true top-5 nearest neighbors of the query. As nprobe grows from 1 to 4, more cells get scanned. Watch recall climb and the candidate-set size climb with it.

If `nprobe = 1`, you only search one cell and the search is fastest, but you miss any true neighbors that happened to sit just across a cell boundary. As `nprobe` grows, you cover more of the space and recall rises. At `nprobe = k`, you've searched everything and you're doing brute force again.

Title: IVF Vector Search: Search Fewer Vectors | M. Hassan Ahmed
URL: https://hassanahmed.net/blog/2026-09-08-ivf-index-vector-search/
Published: 2026-09-08T00:00:00.000Z
Author: Muhammad Hassan Ahmed
Highlights:
The other, which this post is about, is older and simpler to

...

## The flat index does too much work

Do the arithmetic once. A query against a million 768-dimensional vectors is a million dot products of 768 multiply-adds each, on every single search. Modern BLAS (the optimized linear-algebra routines that do this math) makes each one fast, but the total scales with the corpus and never gets cheaper per query. At ten million vectors, you do ten million dot products to answer one question. Most of those comparisons are against vectors that were never going to make the top ten anyway.

That last observation is the whole idea. If the query is about database failover, you do not need to score it against the chunk describing a frontend build error. You only need to look at the neighborhood the query lands in. A flat index has no notion of neighborhood: it treats the corpus as an undifferentiated bag and scans all of it. IVF gives the corpus a coarse structure, so the search can skip most of it.

## Partition first, search locally

IVF has one setup step. Take a sample of your vectors and run k-means to find `nlist` centroids (cluster centers). Those centroids carve the space into `nlist` cells, one per centroid, and every point belongs to the cell of its nearest centroid. Geometrically, the cells form a Voronoi diagram: each boundary falls exactly halfway between two neighboring centroids. FAISS calls the k-means step the coarse quantizer, because it quantizes each vector down to a single id, the id of the cell it lands in.

Then you fill the index. Each vector is assigned to its nearest centroid, and its id is appended to that cell’s posting list. The name “inverted file” is borrowed straight from text search, where an inverted index maps a term to the list of documents containing it (the term’s posting list). Here the “term” is a cell, and the posting list holds the ids of the vectors that fell into it.

Search is where the saving shows up:

1. Compute the distance from the query to the `nlist` centroids.
2. Pick the `nprobe` nearest cells.
3. Scan only the vectors on those cells’ posting lists.

Everything in the other cells is never touched.

The amount of work saved is the point. Instead of `N` comparisons, you do `nlist` to rank the centroids, plus roughly `nprobe × N / nlist` to scan the probed cells (assuming vectors spread evenly). With a million vectors, `nlist = 1024`, and `nprobe = 8`, that is about 1024 + 8,000 comparisons instead of 1,000,000. Two orders of magnitude less work, for an answer that is usually the same.

...

## nprobe is the whole tradeoff

Set `nprobe = 1` and you scan only the single closest cell. That is the fastest possible search, and your recall is whatever fraction of the true neighbors happened to live in that one cell. Raise `nprobe` and you scan more neighboring cells: you catch more of the true neighbors and pay proportionally more time. At `nprobe = nlist` you scan every cell, which is a flat search with extra steps. It is exact again, and slower than a plain flat index, because you also paid for the partitioning.

The shape of those two curves is why IVF is worth the trouble. Recall climbs fast and then saturates, while cost keeps rising with every extra cell you probe and never flattens. Between them sits a knee, usually at a small `nprobe` relative to `nlist`, where you have bought most of the recall for a fraction of the scanning.

Finding that knee is not guesswork. Build the index, hold out a set of queries, and compute their exact neighbors once with a flat index. Then sweep `nprobe` while measuring recall@k against that ground truth. The right `nprobe` is the smallest one that clears your recall target. Nobody can tell you that number from theory; it depends on how your embeddings cluster.

## Where it bites

The happy path is a dozen lines. The failure modes all follow from one fact: IVF draws hard boundaries through a continuous space, and hard boundaries cut through neighborhoods.

The boundary problem is structural, not a bug. A query near the edge of its cell has true neighbors sitting just across the line, in a cell you did not probe. That circled, missed point in the first diagram is not a rare accident; it is the built-in cost of partitioning. Raising `nprobe` shrinks the problem because you probe more of the adjacent cells, which is exactly why recall and `nprobe` move together. Short of scanning every cell, no `nprobe` guarantees you caught everything.

The index has to be trained, and training can go wrong. The centroids come from k-means on a sample. Train on an unrepresentative slice, say the first 10,000 vectors when your corpus is sorted by source, and the cells describe that corner of the space instead of the whole thing. Vectors from the rest of the corpus then pile into a handful of ill-fitting cells while others sit nearly empty, and both speed and recall degrade. Sample across the whole corpus, and give k-means enough points: the FAISS guidance suggests on the order of 30 to 256 training points per centroid.

Cells drift as you add data. The centroids are frozen at train time. If your corpus grows or shifts domain after training, new vectors still get assigned to the old cells, and the partition slowly stops matching the data. It is the same staleness the PQ codebooks have.

...

`nlist` is a sizing decision, not a default. With too few cells, each posting list is long, so probing a cell scans a lot of vectors and you lose the speedup. With too many, each cell is tiny: the coarse quantizer’s own `nlist`-way ranking gets expensive, and you need a larger `nprobe` to gather enough candidates. The common starting point is around `sqrt(N)` cells, tuned from there. A million vectors lands near `nlist = 1024` to `4096`.

The metric has to match the embeddings. IVF inherits whatever distance you configure. Text embeddings are almost always compared with cosine, which means normalizing the vectors and using inner product, as in the code above. Get this wrong and both the k-means partition and the search are measuring in the wrong geometry.

Title: Analysis-Fed highlights economic strength but muddies outlook for Treasuries By Reuters
URL: https://www.investing.com/news/economy-news/analysisfed-highlights-economic-strength-but-muddies-outlook-for-treasuries-4981483
Published: 2026-10-29T05:05:37.000Z
Author: N/A
Highlights:
NEW YORK, Oct 29 (Reuters) - The Federal Reserve kept interest rates steady on Wednesday as expected, but it was not able to comfort bond investors concerned about what a deliberate pace of policy tightening will mean for the outlook for longer-term government bonds.

The central bank described an economy strong enough to keep inflation elevated, yet refrained from raising rates immediately. That deepened uncertainty over how much further policy may need to tighten, analysts said, and over how much compensation investors could demand to hold longer-dated Treasuries, which have soared this year to their highest yields in two decades.

The Fed upgraded its assessment of the economy to "strong" from the "solid" expansion seen as of the September meeting, while describing investment as robust and job gains as keeping pace with the workforce. But how that all leads to price pressures coming down - the main priority for bond investors - was less clear.

"Ultimately, if we see strong growth, which (Fed Chair Kevin) Warsh is expecting, we’re going to see more inflation, which means those fiscal deficit concerns and how to address them longer term become more relevant," said Anders Persson, chief investment officer for global fixed income at investment manager Nuveen in Charlotte, North Carolina.

...

A combination of resilient economic growth and persistent inflation could complicate the US fiscal outlook, limiting the Fed’s ability to lower interest rates when the economy turns and keeping Treasury borrowing costs elevated.

The yield curve steepened following Warsh’s press conference, with the long end selling off. The spread between 2- and 10-year yields widened to as much as 34.1 basis points after flattening over the last few weeks.

There were different interpretations as to why. One was that Warsh did not give a definitive commitment on future policy action, which reduced rate-hike bets. He also suggested the Fed’s last rate increase is starting to work and that financial conditions have started to tighten.

The resulting steepening of the US Treasury yield curve, however, underscores the growing tension between a Fed that is willing to wait for more evidence before adjusting policy and investors increasingly concerned about persistent price pressures and the risks of holding long-term government debt.

Treasury yields have climbed across most maturities from the belly of the curve - between 5 and 7 years - onwards following the Fed’s latest decision, with longer-dated yields coming under particular pressure.

Title: Fed interest rate decision October 2026: Fed holds rates steady
URL: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/28/fed-interest-rate-decision-october-2026.html
Published: 2026-10-28T18:00:18.000Z
Author: Jeff Cox
Highlights:
The Federal Reserve voted Wednesday to keep benchmark interest rates on hold, opting to take a patient approach in its fight against inflation despite mounting evidence that price pressures are proving more nettlesome than policymakers had hoped.

In a widely expected decision, the Federal Open Market Committee kept the overnight funds rate in a range between 3.75%-4%, where it has been since the central bank approved a quarter percentage point increase in September.

"Inflation remains elevated," the post-meeting statement said. "The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability."

## Two voters dissented

Two of the 12 FOMC voters dissented from the decision – Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, both of whom wanted the committee to raise rates by a quarter percentage point.

...

The dissents reflected underlying conflict on the committee over how aggressively it needs to raise rates to combat rising prices. Inflation has been above the Fed's 2% target for more than five years, and the pace of price increases has only picked up since the September meeting.

Statements over the past several weeks, though, have reflected a desire to wait for additional data to come in before tightening policy further. Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams both said current economic conditions allow policymakers time to evaluate their next move.

The statement characterized economic activity as "expanding at a strong pace," a seeming upgrade from "solid" in September. There were no other substantial changes to the statement other than the removal of a sentence that explained the September increase.

The decision came as little surprise as markets had been pricing in a less than 10% chance of a hike, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Following the decision, the S&P 500 held on to its gains. 

However, it raises fresh questions about how long policymakers are willing to wait before tightening again. Futures market pricing indicates a strong possibility of another hike at the next FOMC meeting in December, and perhaps another increase or two in 2027.

...

## Complicated economic picture

The Fed is up against a complicated economic and political picture. Inflation as measured by the Fed's preferred gauge is expected to be above 3% for September, even when excluding volatile food and energy prices. Economists are concerned that inflation has broadened beyond the energy sector and the impact from the Iran war.

At the same time, the unemployment rate has remained low and economic growth has been strong. The Atlanta Fed's GDPNow tracker is pointing to 3.4% annualized growth in the third quarter, which would be the strongest in a year. Consumer spending also has been solid, and investment tied to the artificial intelligence boom has helped keep the U.S. economic engine running.

The combination, though, has added to debate about how much restriction the Fed's current interest rate is actually exerting on the economy, and whether policymakers will need to move more aggressively if the price data doesn't improve.

While markets expect additional hikes, Warsh has avoided providing so-called forward guidance about the FOMC's intentions. In June, his fellow committee members, through the "dot plot" grid, indicated the likelihood of another increase this year.

"The Fed is taking a wait-and-see approach, and I think that makes sense given where we are in the cycle," said Andrew Davis, head of investment strategy at Bryn Mawr Trust and a former BLS analyst. "The economy is slowing, but slowing and breaking are two different things. Holding rates steady gives policymakers more time to assess how the economy is responding to September's hike and the recent rise in longer-term borrowing costs."

The experiment utilizes two sets of QA pairs extracted from the Nature Question[13] dataset to construct a basic knowledge base containing 3k question-answer pairs and 88k question-answer pairs for a large knowledge base. To evaluate the performance of the retrieval system, the dataset was divided into four groups for testing:

Scenario A: A set of 100 randomly selected question-answer pairs from the general knowledge base, used as benchmark testing data.

Scenario B: A set of 100 questions randomly selected from the basic knowledge base, with modifications applied to alter their surface expression while retaining semantic equivalence. This group was designed to assess the system’s robustness in handling variations in question formulation.

For scenario C and Scenario D, the same procedure was followed by exchange of the basic knowledge base with the large base.

### 3.2 Algorithm and Model

The following retrieval algorithms were selected for the experiments:

Sparse Retrieval Algorithms: BM25 and TF-IDF. BM25 is a weighted algorithm based on the frequency of the term and the frequency of the document, while TF-IDF assesses the importance of words within a document.

Dense Retrieval Algorithms: The E5 series models, including E5-Small-V2[8], E5-Base-V2[6], and E5-Large-V2[7]. These models generate dense sentence embeddings for semantic matching, aiming to improve retrieval performance for synonymously expressed queries.

...

This study designed three sets of experiments to systematically evaluate the performance of different retrieval and inference combinations:

Sparse Retrieval Test: BM25 and TF-IDF were applied to the experimental test data for sparse retrieval, and their performance was evaluated.

Dense Retrieval Test: The E5 series models (E5-Small-V2, E5-Base-V2, E5-Large-V2) were employed for dense retrieval on the experimental test data, comparing the performance of each model.

...

To evaluate the retrieval algorithms, the primary focus was on two key accuracy metrics: Recall and Rank Precision.

...

### 4.1 Retrieval

In scenario A and B where the knowledge base is relatively small, the recall rates of both sparse and dense retrieval algorithms are comparable. However, dense retrieval algorithms exhibit greater stability in performance.

...

From a resource efficiency standpoint, sparse retrieval algorithms present a significant advantage. As Table 1 shows, They require only about one-third of the memory resources used by dense retrieval methods. Given the lower computational complexity of sparse retrieval, these algorithms perform similarly to dense retrieval in non-GPU environments. Sparse retrieval also benefits from reduced latency, approximately half that of the smallest dense models, while memory usage is around one-tenth, making it a highly effective choice in resource-constrained systems. In contrast, when sufficient GPU resources are available, dense retrieval algorithms exhibit superior performance, with average latency less than one-third of those for sparse retrieval. This suggests that in designing RAG systems, dense retrieval should be prioritized when ample GPU resources are available, as it provides enhanced recall performance with minimal computational delays.

In the current application scenario, the results of both sparse retrieval algorithms are quite similar. However, the TF-IDF algorithm, which calculates weights solely based on the term frequency and the inverse document frequency, does not take document length into account. This limitation can lead to an overestimation of relevance for longer documents, which poses a problem given that the content in the test knowledge base consists of documents of varying lengths. Ignoring document length can result in imbalanced results and impact the overall accuracy of the retrieval process.

BM25, on the other hand, addresses this issue by normalizing document length and optimizing the handling of term frequency saturation. Specifically, it reduces the weight assigned to terms with extremely high frequencies, preventing these terms from disproportionately influencing the relevance scores. In addition to improving retrieval accuracy, this adjustment also reduces computational latency, contributing positively to the algorithm’s efficiency and complexity.

...

In scenario B, we observed that for fuzzy searches, the precision of BM25 consistently outperformed that of TF-IDF. The randomness in word choice can significantly affect term frequency, leading to increased volatility in document relevance scores. This variability can subsequently reduce the overall performance of the retrieval algorithm. As a result, BM25 offers advantages in certain performance metrics, resulting in better accuracy and overall performance.

In dense retrieval, being deep learning-based models that represent text as high-dimensional embedding vectors to capture semantic information, have demonstrated good adaptability when addressing fuzzy word searches, exhibiting only minor performance degradation. This is illustrated in Table 1 and Table 2.

...

For scenario C and D, with the expansion of the knowledge base, additional memory and GPU resources must be allocated, leading to increased inference times. In the view of system design, it is crucial to consider the upper limits of system latency imposed by the knowledge base size. For larger knowledge bases, sparse retrieval algorithms experience a significant increase in latency, diminishing their overall performance.

When dealing with large datasets, the inherent limitations of sparse algorithms become more pronounced, particularly in handling fuzzy queries. In contrast, dense retrieval algorithms exhibit superior performance and accuracy under these conditions, which makes them better suited for fuzzy queries in RAG systems. Thus, as the knowledge base scales, dense retrieval proves to be a more efficient and accurate solution for managing complex queries in large-scale environments.

Title: Old IR Methods Meet RAG | Proceedings of the 47th International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval
URL: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3626772.3657935
Published: 2024-07-11T00:00:00.000Z
Author: Authors : Oz Huly, Idan Pogrebinsky, David Carmel, Oren Kurland, Yoelle Maarek
Highlights:
SIGIR '24: Proceedings of the 47th International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval

...

### Abstract

Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) is an important approach to provide large language models (LLMs) with context pertaining to the text generation task: given a prompt, passages are retrieved from external corpora to ground the generation with more relevant and/or fresher data. Most previous studies used dense retrieval methods for applying RAG in question answering scenarios. However, recent work showed that traditional information retrieval methods (a.k.a. sparse methods) can do as well as or even better than dense retrieval ones. In particular, it was shown that Okapi BM25 outperforms dense retrieval methods, in terms of perplexity, for the fundamental text completion task in LLMs. We extend this study and show, using two popular LLMs, that a broad set of sparse retrieval methods achieve better results than all the dense retrieval methods we experimented with, for varying lengths of queries induced from the prompt. Furthermore, we found that Okapi BM25 is substantially outperformed by a term-proximity retrieval method (MRF), which is in turn outperformed by a pseudo-feedback-based bag-of-terms approach (relevance model). Additional exploration sheds some light on the effectiveness of lexical retrieval methods for RAG. Our findings call for further study of classical retrieval methods for RAG.
